source: Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern valuation lecture notes (valpacket1spr20 p.298-348, valpacket1spr21 p.292-357) and the Motley Fool valuation deck (valuationmotleyfool p.26)
refresh: https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/ — lecture-note packets and the accompanying spreadsheets. These are published outputs of Damodaran's own simulations, so they do not go stale the way a spread table does; they are dated because each one is a snapshot of a company at a moment, and the market prices in particular are only meaningful at that date. Re-read the source before quoting a case in a live valuation, and add newer cases rather than editing these.
purpose: Calibration anchors and test vectors. This file is reference material, not an input to a valuation. The script never recomputes these numbers; it uses the percentile tables to test the price-location arithmetic and the Shell regression to test the linear map.

paytm_2021.context: Valued ahead of the September 2021 IPO. 100,000 trials.
paytm_2021.finding: Equity was worthless in about 3% of trials. The simulated median sat 14% below the base-case DCF, and the 10th-to-90th range ran from 627,263 to 2,010,052 — a point estimate inside that spread is not a precise claim about value.

amazon_2018.context: Simulation run on the September 2018 DCF.
amazon_2018.finding: The $1,970 market price sat in the top fifth of the simulated distribution. Overvalued in most scenarios, but not in all of them — a different proposition from overvalued everywhere.

shell_2016.context: An oil-price-neutral valuation: the company valued at the market price of oil, with the macro view stated separately as a distribution over that price.

revenue_regression.formula: Revenues ($m) = intercept + slope x average oil price per barrel
revenue_regression.note: An R-squared of 96.44% means the oil price essentially is the revenue model. Simulating the oil price and mapping it through this line is the whole simulation for a commodity firm.

input_distributions.driver: Tax rate, revenue growth, cost of capital

shell_2016.finding: Two drivers, one of them macro, produce a 10th-to-90th range of $23.90 to $57.49 around a $39.31 point estimate. This is the archetype for a commodity or cyclical company where one macro variable dominates.

sp500_2020.context: An index valuation on augmented dividends, simulated. Shows the same machinery applied to a macro object rather than a company.

input_distributions.driver: Share of lost earnings recouped by 2024
Cash returned as a percent of earnings in 2020
input_distributions.correlation: -0.50 with earnings; weaker earnings mean less cash returned

sp500_2020.finding: The index traded at 3,270, between the 70th and 80th percentiles. The market was at the upper-middle of the plausible range rather than obviously wrong. Note the two signed correlations: earnings across years positively, payout against earnings negatively.
